analysis.one_liner: Requires FDA premarket review for all e-cigarettes and orders recall of unreviewed vapes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee with no cosponsors at the end of the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write e-cigarettes and vape pens into federal law as tobacco products and require every one of them to pass a Food and Drug Administration safety review before being sold. Any vape product that had not gone through that review would have to be recalled from stores within 60 days of the law taking effect. It received no committee action and expired when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, especially young people, would benefit from fewer unreviewed vape products on store shelves. The bill would force any vape device or liquid without FDA premarket authorization off the market within 60 days, with a public notice to users about the risks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Young people and vape users' families

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to define 'electronic nicotine delivery system' as a tobacco product, covering e-cigarettes, e-hookahs, vape pens, e-cigars, electronic pipes, and their liquids and parts, whether or not sold separately [S3].

It requires the FDA, within 60 days of enactment, to order manufacturers, importers, distributors, and retailers to stop distributing and recall any vape product that has not received premarket authorization, with a timetable, progress reports, notice to users, and an opportunity for an informal hearing [S3].

It blocks any exemption: beginning 60 days after enactment, all vape products are deemed not substantially equivalent to older tobacco products and must undergo premarket review under section 910 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Vape manufacturers, importers, distributors, and retailers would bear the cost, since products lacking FDA authorization could no longer be sold. Adults who vape would lose access to products that had not cleared review, and the FDA would face the workload of processing recalls and applications.
analysis.who_pays_short: Vape makers, sellers, and adult vapers

drawbacks.text: A mandatory recall within 60 days could pull products off shelves that many adults use in place of cigarettes, before the FDA has finished reviewing the applications already pending for those products; the bill's text sets no transition beyond the 60-day clock [S3].
Removing legal flavored and unreviewed vapes quickly risks pushing sales to an unregulated black market that has no age checks or ingredient disclosure at all.

The bill leaves the practical burden on the FDA to identify and recall a large number of products on short notice, and retailers who cannot be identified would be notified through general public notice instead [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health case is real: most vape products on the market at the time had never gone through the FDA premarket review the bill would mandate, and youth vaping was a top concern. But the bill's hard 60-day recall deadline is blunt, and an honest supporter would acknowledge the cost to adult smokers and vapers who relied on products the FDA had not yet ruled on. A slower transition period would have softened that trade-off.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Mark DeSaulnier introduced the Preventing Vape Use Act on June 23, 2022, near the end of the two-year congressional session [S1][S5].
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, which is where bills on tobacco and FDA policy go; no further action was ever recorded [S5].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S4], and the committee never scheduled a hearing or markup before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Vape manufacturers and retailers, who kept selling unreviewed products, and adult vapers who kept access to them; no one else gained much, since the bill was too late in the session and had no cosponsors to build momentum.

for.name: Rep. Mark DeSaulnier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; no other member joined him

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the remainder of the 117th Congress

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so no party split is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have required a recall within 60 days of every vape product without FDA premarket authorization, which at the time covered most of the market. The industry's interest in keeping unreviewed products on shelves ran against the public-health goal of subjecting them to review.

Retailers and distributors would have been ordered to stop selling and pull unreviewed vape products, cutting off a significant product line. Consumers seeking the products would have had fewer legal options.
